q: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs `fn` on the very next line of your code.
why: No. `setTimeout` only says "call this later". `fn` waits until the call stack is empty, and until every promise callback has run.

q: Who does the waiting for a `setTimeout` timer or a `fetch` request?
options: The browser (Web APIs), not JavaScript
The call stack, which pauses until the timer is done
The microtask queue
A second JavaScript thread
why: JavaScript has one chef and does not wait. The browser keeps the timer on the side and puts the callback in a queue when it is done.

q: A promise is already done and you call `.then(fn)` on it. Where does `fn` wait before it runs?
options: In the microtask queue
In the task queue, behind the timers
In the browser Web APIs
On the call stack, so it runs at once
why: Promise callbacks wait in the microtask queue. It is a faster waiting line that is emptied before the next task.

q: Which of these callbacks wait in the microtask queue, so they run before the next timer?
options: The `.then` callback of a promise that is already done
The callback of `setTimeout(fn, 0)`
The code after an `await`
The callback of a button click
why: Promise callbacks and the code after `await` are microtasks. Timers and clicks are tasks, and tasks wait until all microtasks are done.

q: Put the letters in the order this code prints them.
why: A and D are plain code, so they run first. Then the microtask C. Then the task B. The rule: sync code, then microtasks, then one task.

q: What does this print? Type the three letters in order, with spaces between them.
why: `z` is plain code, so it runs first. Then the microtask `y`. The timer `x` is a task, so it comes last.

q: The event loop empties the whole microtask queue before it takes the next task, even when a microtask adds a new microtask.
why: Yes. That is why `c` and `d` in the lesson's practice A both run before the first timer. A microtask that adds another microtask just joins the same emptying.

q: Put one turn of the event loop in the right order.
items: The plain code runs until the call stack is empty
One task runs, for example a timer callback
The loop goes back to the microtasks
why: Sync code first, then every microtask, then exactly one task. After that task the loop looks at the microtasks again before it takes another task.

options: `fn` runs after at least 100 ms, when the call stack is free
`fn` runs after exactly 100 ms
`fn` runs within 100 ms, before the next task
`fn` pauses the code for 100 ms, then runs
why: The time is a minimum. If the stack is busy, `fn` waits longer. A timer of 0 ms means "at least 0 ms", not "now".

q: What does this print? Type the five numbers in order, with spaces between them.
why: `1` and `5` are plain code. Then both microtasks run, `3` and then `4` (it is added while the microtasks are being emptied). The timer `2` comes last.

q: Which of these can stop timers and clicks from running for a while?
options: A `while` loop that runs for 3 seconds
A `fetch` request that takes 5 seconds to answer
A promise callback that keeps adding a new promise callback forever
A `setTimeout` of 5000 ms
why: A long loop keeps the stack busy. Endless microtasks never let a task or a screen update have its turn. A `fetch` or a timer is waited on by the browser, not by JavaScript, so it blocks nothing.

q: A `while` loop keeps the stack busy for 300 ms. A timer of 0 ms was set just before it. When does the timer callback run?
options: After the loop is finished, about 300 ms late
At once, because the browser runs it in parallel
Never, because the loop cancels the timer
Between two turns of the loop
why: A callback can only start when the call stack is empty. A long loop blocks the timers and the clicks too.

options: `return user` runs before the timer callback, so `user` is still empty
`setTimeout` deletes the `user` variable
A timer of 0 ms is ignored by JavaScript
`let` variables cannot be changed inside a callback
why: The timer callback waits for the stack to empty, so it runs after `return`. Return a promise instead, so the caller can wait for the value.
